messages.subject: advice about a model with mean dependent variance
parts:
Hello,
I'm trying to fit a model given by J groups of observations, and the data within each group is generated according to a normal distribution with an unknown mean and  standard deviation is a linear function of the mean, with unknown slope and intercept. 
I want to use "non-informative" priors for all parameters (below I use normal priors with large variance) and I get some problems.
The group means are positive and far from 0 (say >100), and the slope and intercept of the linear relation are constrained to be positive, therefore this guarantees a positive standard deviation.
Below is an example with simulated data. I observe the following issues:

- The Heidelberger-Welch convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter
- The Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter (upper bound of shriink factor > 1.05)
- The 95%-credibilty interval often fail to contain the true value for slope and intercept
- I'm under the impression that convergence does not occur for slope and intercept when looking at the running means (ggs_running(ggsamples, "slope")) 

I'd like to have any advice about what I do. Does the model seems sensible to you ? Is there something to do for imrpoving the convergence ?

messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] advice about a model with mean dependent variance
parts:
Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
so far away from standardized.

I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
than hardcoding the priors.

mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.

Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:
> mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)

and then the prior is:

> mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);

This requires the data to pull the posterior
3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
are only providing 6 data points per group. That's
unlikely to work. Usually we're urging people to use
more informative priors, not less informative ones.

As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
a pull to 200.

I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
simulation matches your model. I find it easier when the
R code variable names match those in the model. But this
looks fishy:

> for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> + dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> + }

because there's nothing like it in the model. Why
are you rounding it down? Do you really want to be
fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
a negative binomial?

This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:

> intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> slope <- exp(logslope);
> for(j in 1:J) {

> sigma[j] <- exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> }

You're better off replacing the last line with:

sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;

and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:

vector<lower=0>[J] mu;

Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.

real<lower=0> slope;
real<lower=0> intercept;

This would require reformulating the priors.

You can also replace this:

> for(j in 1:J){
> + mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> + }

with the much more efficient

mu ~ normal(200,30);

- Bob

Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
so far away from standardized.

I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
than hardcoding the priors.  

  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.

Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:

> mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)

and then the prior is:

> mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);

This requires the data to pull the posterior
3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
more informative priors, not less informative ones.

As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
a pull to 200.

I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
looks fishy:

> for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> + }

because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
a negative binomial?

This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:

>    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
>    slope <- exp(logslope);
>    for(j in 1:J) {
>      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
>    }


You're better off replacing the last line with:

  sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;

and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:

  vector<lower=0>[J] mu;

Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.

  real<lower=0> slope;
  real<lower=0> intercept;

This would require reformulating the priors.

You can also replace this:

> for(j in 1:J){
> +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> +   }


with the much more efficient

  mu ~ normal(200,30);

The terminology is confusing.

lognormal is the lognormal distribution. It has positive
support. The function is called lognormal_log, because
it evaluates the lognormal density on the log scale.

normal_log is just the standard normal density evaluated
on the log scale.

parts: Hello Bob,

I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather 
than hardcoding the priors.   
  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Do you have some recommandation for the hyperpriors ? Currently I'm using something like that :

bigmu ~ normal(5, 20);
bigsigma ~ gamma(.002,.001);
mu ~ lognormal(bigmu, bigsigma);

My mu[i] range from 100 to 300, the prior on bigmu largely covers this range.  And the prior on bigsigma largely covers the expected standard deviation of the posterior distributions of the mu[i].
Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
so far away from standardized. llo Bob,

I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
than hardcoding the priors.  

  mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);

Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.

Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:

> mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)

and then the prior is:

> mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);

This requires the data to pull the posterior
3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
are only providing 6 data points per group.  That's
unlikely to work.  Usually we're urging people to use
more informative priors, not less informative ones.

As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
a pull to 200.

I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
simulation matches your model.  I find it easier when the
R code variable names match those in the model.  But this
looks fishy:

> for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> +   dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> + }

because there's nothing like it in the model.  Why
are you rounding it down?  Do you really want to be
fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
a negative binomial?

This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:

>    intercept <- exp(logintercept);
>    slope <- exp(logslope);
>    for(j in 1:J) {
>      sigma[j] <-  exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
>    }


You're better off replacing the last line with:

  sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;

and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:

  vector<lower=0>[J] mu;

Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.

  real<lower=0> slope;
  real<lower=0> intercept;

This would require reformulating the priors.

You can also replace this:

> for(j in 1:J){
> +     mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> +   }


with the much more efficient

  mu ~ normal(200,30);

- Bob

parts:
Unlike lower-level priors, the hyperpriors have never seemed
very sensitive in anything I've done, so as long as you cover
the expected range, you should be OK. The closer you can get
without being too restrictive, the better things will be
computationally.

I would stay away from those super-diffuse gammas --- there's
a discussion of priors in the manual chapter on regression (multiple
sections), and references to Andrew's papers on why not to use
the BUGS-standard (inverse) gamma distributions.

- Bob

> On Feb 25, 2015, at 8:09 PM, 'Stéphane Laurent' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
>
> Hello Bob,
>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
> mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Do you have some recommandation for the hyperpriors ? Currently I'm using something like that :
>
> bigmu ~ normal(5, 20);
> bigsigma ~ gamma(.002,.001);
> mu ~ lognormal(bigmu, bigsigma);
>
> My mu[i] range from 100 to 300, the prior on bigmu largely covers this range. And the prior on bigsigma largely covers the expected standard deviation of the posterior distributions of the mu[i].
>
>
>
>
> Le mercredi 18 février 2015 14:23:12 UTC+1, Bob Carpenter a écrit :
> Stan may need more warmup to adapt to data scales
> so far away from standardized. llo Bob,
>
>
> I'd suggest fitting a hierarchical model rather
> than hardcoding the priors.
>
> mu ~ normal(mu_mu, sigma_mu);
>
> Then you won't have to guess at the prior scales.
>
> Taking your model at face value, your simulation has:
>
> > mu <- seq(100, 300, len=J)
>
> and then the prior is:
>
> > mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
>
> This requires the data to pull the posterior
> 3+ standard deviations away from the prior, but you
> are only providing 6 data points per group. That's
> unlikely to work. Usually we're urging people to use
> more informative priors, not less informative ones.
>
> As you can see in your fit, you're getting too strong
> a pull to 200.
>
> I can't read R fluently enough to tell if your
> simulation matches your model. I find it easier when the
> R code variable names match those in the model. But this
> looks fishy:
>
> > for(i in 1:nrow(dat)){
> > + dat$y[i] <- floor(rnorm(1, dat$mu[i], a+b*dat$mu[i]))
> > + }
>
> because there's nothing like it in the model. Why
> are you rounding it down? Do you really want to be
> fitting a discrete model with overdispersion, like
> a negative binomial?
>
> This code isn't wrong, but it's very inefficient:
>
> > intercept <- exp(logintercept);
> > slope <- exp(logslope);
> > for(j in 1:J) {
> > sigma[j] <- exp(logintercept)+exp(logslope)*mu[j];
> > }
>
>
> You're better off replacing the last line with:
>
> sigma <- intercept + slope * mu;
>
> and changing the declaration of mu to be a vector:
>
> vector<lower=0>[J] mu;
>
> Rather than putting all the transforms in the model,
> you might want to try just using the built-in constraints.
>
> real<lower=0> slope;
> real<lower=0> intercept;
>
> This would require reformulating the priors.
>
> You can also replace this:
>
> > for(j in 1:J){
> > + mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);
> > + }
>
>
> with the much more efficient
>
> mu ~ normal(200,30);
>
> - Bob
>
> > On Feb 18, 2015, at 10:24 PM, 'Stéphane Laurent' via Stan users mailing list <stan-...@googlegroups.com> wrote:
> >
> > Hello,
> > I'm trying to fit a model given by J groups of observations, and the data within each group is generated according to a normal distribution with an unknown mean and standard deviation is a linear function of the mean, with unknown slope and intercept.
> > I want to use "non-informative" priors for all parameters (below I use normal priors with large variance) and I get some problems.
> > The group means are positive and far from 0 (say >100), and the slope and intercept of the linear relation are constrained to be positive, therefore this guarantees a positive standard deviation.
> > Below is an example with simulated data. I observe the following issues:
> >
> > - The Heidelberger-Welch convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter
> > - The Gelman-Rubin convergence diagnostic often fails for the slope parameter (upper bound of shriink factor > 1.05)
> > - The 95%-credibilty interval often fail to contain the true value for slope and intercept
> > - I'm under the impression that convergence does not occur for slope and intercept when looking at the running means (ggs_running(ggsamples, "slope"))
> >
> > I'd like to have any advice about what I do. Does the model seems sensible to you ? Is there something to do for imrpoving the convergence ?

> > + }
> > + model {

> > + y[i] ~ normal(mu[group[i]], sigma[group[i]]);
> > + }
> > + for(j in 1:J){
> > + mu[j] ~ normal(200,30);

> > + logintercept ~ normal(0,10);
> > + logslope ~ normal(0,10);

> > + "
